title: The World Council of Churches (1948)
hookLine: churches from many traditions meet to pray and work together

lines: THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.
cards: Much of Europe is in ruins, in the years just after the Second World War.

Churches that had prayed on opposite sides of the war send people to Amsterdam: Protestants and Anglicans, Orthodox churches of the East, delegates from Asia, Africa and the Americas. They pray together. They argue.
And they decide to form a council and keep meeting. Behind it is a prayer. In John's Gospel, on the night before he dies, Jesus prays for his followers: "That they all may be one."
Christians have read those words aloud in churches that, for long stretches, would not share a table, a pulpit or a cup.

teach.b: First, what the World Council of Churches is not. It isn't a super-church. Nobody leaves their own church to join it, and it doesn't tell its members what to believe.

It describes itself as a fellowship of churches that confess Jesus Christ as God and Savior, according to the scriptures, and try together to live out that calling. Each church keeps its own worship, leaders and teaching.
They meet as guests at one table. The message from that first gathering in Amsterdam is remembered for a simple resolve: the churches meant to stay together. Not merge.
Stay. Second, who sits at the table. Protestant and Anglican churches, and Orthodox churches of the East, are among its members.
The Catholic Church isn't a member, but it has worked alongside the council, and each year the two together prepare the materials for a week of prayer for Christian unity.

teach.h: SOME STAY OUTSIDE, FOR REAL REASONS.
teach.b: Some churches stay outside altogether, for reasons they take seriously: a worry that unity could blur what they believe, or a different understanding of what the church is.
Those are honest convictions, not failures of goodwill. Third, what they do.

They pray. They study hard questions, like baptism and communion, side by side, and write down where they agree and where they don't. And they work: refugees, relief after disasters, peace talks, hunger.
Jesus's prayer is a prayer, not a plan. The council is one attempt to take it seriously, with all the slowness real agreement takes.

how: Member churches send delegates to the council's assemblies and committees, and in some towns local churches of different traditions keep a week of prayer for Christian unity together.

games.q: you're a church delegate in Amsterdam after the war. your church disagrees with others in the room about baptism and communion. what do you do?
o: walk out until everyone agrees with you.
stay at the table, pray together, and study the differences side by side.
games.why: the gathering resolved to stay together without merging, and to work through hard questions together over time.

practice: Think of a church that isn't yours: the Orthodox parish with the onion domes, the storefront church with the hand-painted sign, the cathedral downtown.
Picture the people who will gather there this week, their kitchen, their choir, their worries.
If you pray, borrow Jesus's words for them and for you, that they all may be one; if you don't, simply wish them well, by name if you know it.

wordCard.voice: Amsterdam, the city where churches met after the war and formed a fellowship that still meets to pray, study and work together, each keeping its own life.

orig.note: Greek: the whole inhabited world; the word behind 'ecumenical', used for efforts toward Christian unity.

carryVoice: Your line: together. Not merging, just staying, as guests at one table. See you tomorrow.
